summary.text:
This note now covers two Hackney treasury papers. The primary reading (16 August 2026) is the Council's own Appendix 3 — Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27, approved by Council on 4 March 2026 (doc 96978). The secondary reading (15 August 2026) is the Pension Fund Treasury Management Strategy 2026-2029, heard at Pensions Committee on 30 March 2026 (docs 97651 + 97652); that paper is non-addressable by PWLBtoday because the Fund does not borrow (cover §4.4) and every fact about the Council's balance sheet sits in the Council TMS.

The Council TMS is one of the largest borrowing ramps we have read. The Capital Financing Requirement rises from £626m at March 2025 to £1,520m by March 2029 — 143% growth in four years, driven by regeneration and HRA capital delivery. Existing external borrowing of £310.05m at 31 December 2025 is projected to shrink to £145m by March 2029 as short-term debt rolls off; against that, the paper's own summary is a cumulative net new borrowing requirement of about £1,018m over the strategy period. Total external debt is therefore on track to move from £310m today to around £1,163m by March 2029 — nearly a quadrupling.

The most striking treasury choice is the tightening of the maturity-structure limits (Table 10). The previous 0-100% ceilings have been replaced with 40 / 40 / 60 / 60 / 80 upper limits by bucket, and the commentary is explicit that this is to control refinancing risk BEFORE the borrowing programme runs. Paragraph 7.6 then commits the 2026/27 long-term borrowing decision to a breakeven and cost-of-carry analysis against Arlingclose's forecast — a forecast, printed in Appendix A, that assumed Bank Rate would fall from 3.75% to 3.25% by Q2 2026 and long-end gilts would drift slightly lower by September 2026. Neither happened. Bank Rate has held at 3.75%, the 10-year gilt is about 0.78 above the September 2026 central case, and the 50-year is about 1.02 above.

Balance-sheet identity holds cleanly across every year of Table 2: CFR = external borrowing + OLTL + internal borrowing. The loan-book reconciliation, however, does NOT tie — the paper reports £310.05m total external at 3.67% weighted (of which £246m long-term, per §7.7 all PWLB), and our own PWLB file for Hackney holds only 11 loans totalling £163.3m at 3.74% weighted at the same date. The likeliest cause is that our file is not capturing pre-2025 tranches (no PWLB loans appear in our file for Hackney before October 2025). Reconciliation is therefore kept out of the email entirely per PIPELINE.md, and the strategy angle stands on its own.

Paper 96978 carries no officer name. The S151 role sits with the Group Director Finance and Corporate Resources (Naeem Ahmed per the Pension Fund paper 97651 front sheet); no address is published for him in either paper. Deidre Worrell, Director Financial Management, has a published address on the Pension Fund paper (deidre.worrell@hackney.gov.uk) and signed the financial implications on behalf of the Group Director — she is a legitimate Council finance recipient. Draft is written for the mid-year audit-committee treasury update expected in autumn 2026, addressed to Deidre Worrell.

reconciliation.against: Council Appendix 3 — Treasury Management Strategy 2026/27 (doc 96978), Table 1 at 31 December 2025
reconciliation.note: DOES NOT TIE. Paper Table 1 (31/12/25): total external borrowing £310.05m at 3.67% weighted; §6.4 splits into £1.05m Hackney Green crowdfund + £63m short-term + £246m long-term, with §7.7 stating that all long-term borrowing has historically been raised from the PWLB. Our PWLB file for Hackney at 31/12/2025: 11 loans, £163,328,070 principal, weighted rate 3.7412%. Gap on the PWLB comparison (paper £246m vs ours £163m) is £83m; on the total external comparison the gap is £147m. Rate differs by 7bp (paper 3.67% vs ours 3.74%). The most likely explanation is that our PWLB file is not capturing pre-October-2025 tranches — price_book.py returns 'No loans outstanding' at 30 September 2025 and earlier for Hackney, which is not credible for a London borough that took ~£246m of HRA self-financing PWLB in 2012. Kept out of the email in full — no 'we hold N loans totalling £X at Y%' claim is made. Our figures are recorded in the internal block below.

officer.body:
Hi Deidre,

Apologies for the cold email. PWLBtoday is fairly new so you may not have come across us yet.

We're built for local authority treasury teams and nothing else: live PWLB rates at both daily fixings, a monthly breakdown of every loan the sector draws, every council's PWLB book priced daily against the DMO's repayment curve, and a training academy for officers and members. There's more — the predictor, the SONIA path, peer metrics, a daily brief — in the brochure at [BROCHURE URL]. We don't sell treasury products, and the data side is free and stays free.

To keep that data and our training relevant we built tools that watch committee papers across every council in the country, so we can see how a council's own figures compare with where the market has gone since. So below are a few thoughts on your 2026/27 Treasury Management Strategy, the one that went to Council on 4 March, read now against where the curve has moved. You're not being singled out — every authority gets one of these — and there's no agenda in it.

One thing up front on our own data. Paragraph 6.4 sets out £246m of long-term borrowing inside the £310.05m at 31 December 2025, and 7.7 says the Council has raised all its long-term borrowing from the PWLB. Our own PWLB file for Hackney holds less than that at the same date — we're probably not yet capturing the older HRA self-financing tranches — so nothing below is a comparison of your book against ours, and the appendix is authoritative. It's the kind of gap a next audit-committee update, with a printed loan table, will let us close.

What stands out is the shape of what's ahead. Table 2 has the Loan CFR moving £566m to £1,495m between March 2025 and March 2029, and the paper's own chart caption on page 5 puts the cumulative net new borrowing requirement at about £1,018m over the strategy period, against a projected £145m of existing external debt still on the book by then. Table 10 looks right for that programme — you've tightened the maturity limits from the previous 100% ceilings to 40, 40, 60, 60, 80, and the commentary is explicit that this is refinancing control put in place before the borrowing runs, not after. That's uncommon forward discipline in what we've read and worth calling out.

The testable point is the forecast the strategy sits on. Arlingclose's December 2025 central case, in Appendix A, has Bank Rate falling from 3.75% to 3.25% by Q2 2026, the 10-year gilt at 4.25% by September 2026, and the 50-year at 4.45%. Where we are on 14 August: Bank Rate has held at 3.75% — the further cut didn't happen — and the 1-year OIS is at 4.11%, so the market is now pricing the next move up rather than down. The 10-year gilt sits about 0.78 above the September central case and the 50-year about 1.02 above. None of that changes the strategy Council has already approved. Paragraph 7.6 says Arlingclose will help with the breakeven and cost-of-carry work on whether to borrow additional sums at long-term fixed rates in 2026/27. The rate you're running that calculation against has moved a long way from the December forecast.

The tool we'd point you to for that is pwlbtoday.org/loan-analysis (the daily curve, both fixings, certainty and standard, HRA rate, NWF, and every PWLB book we hold priced against the DMO's repayment curve) and pwlbtoday.org/pwlb-activity for the monthly sector view — July was £368m across 33 loans from just 19 borrowers at an average 5.02%. The interactive liability benchmark pathway at pwlbtoday.org/liability-benchmark plots the shape you've got in Table 3 against every other LB we hold; worth a look ahead of CIPFA's forthcoming updates to the Prudential and Treasury Codes, and particularly for a council whose LB rises to £1,278m by 2028/29 before amortising out to 2075.

On the caveats: we hold PWLB only — LOBOs, market debt, bank loans and inter-authority borrowing all sit outside our file (and, as flagged, our historic PWLB may itself be incomplete for Hackney). Any break-cost figure we publish is indicative only against the DMO's premature repayment curve; only the DMO's own quote is binding. We model no MRP or accounting treatment.

On training, three feel relevant. Cost of carry and internal borrowing, since the strategy is a transition from historic internal borrowing to a borrowing-led approach and 7.6 makes the cost-of-carry call the pivotal 2026/27 decision. Liability Benchmark: the essentials, given the £1,278m Mar-29 peak and the amortising tail behind it. And Prudential Indicators for members, since Council votes directly on the operational boundary stepping from £1,196m in 2026/27 to £1,580m in 2028/29. All 115 courses are free to local authorities until the end of September at pwlbtoday.org/academy, and free accounts for the whole team.

And if you do find it useful, mentioning it to others would help us more than anything. We're small, word of mouth is most of our marketing, and every sign-up helps us prove the need.

Sign up free → https://pwlbtoday.org/
Follow on LinkedIn → https://www.linkedin.com/company/pwlbtoday/
